The keyed bugle appeared at the beginning of the nineteenth century, and the Englishman Joseph Halliday took out a patent in 1811, calling it the Kent bugle. It entered British and American military music, with many tutors and arrangements, and was widely used until about 1850, after which it was mostly replaced by the cornet; Richard Willis, the first bandmaster of the West Point band, wrote for it and played it. After the middle of the nineteenth century the bugle generally changed to piston valves.

The keyed bugle is a keyed variant developed from the bugle at the beginning of the nineteenth century; it is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 423.121.22. It consists mainly of a conical tube and a mouthpiece, and the player controls pitch with the lips and the breath; an ordinary bugle can sound only the few notes of the harmonic series, and the keys serve to change the pitch. The source mentions that the Englishman Joseph Halliday took out a patent in 1811, calling it the Kent bugle, and that it was widely used in British and American military bands, with tutors and arrangements.
